title: Jim Robinson, Percy Humphrey and playing softly to an audience
summary: Anecdotes about Jim Robinson drinking his way home, his playing, and Percy Humphrey's quiet muted solo that won the crowd.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: It was so funny meeting Jim Robinson on the street. We were walking over to Kid Howard's house. And Jim had just stopped by Willie Parker's house. And what did he play? I'm alone because I love you. The Willie Parker. Because he walked out of the street after finishing playing with the Onward Brass pad. Then we met him. And so what did he play? About four bars of You Tell Me Your Dreams. He was just gradually drinking his way home.

Beautiful. It was marvellous. It reminds me of the sort of people we get sometimes in the audience in Australia, who have quite a few drinks and come up and say, play some Irish songs. That sort of thing.
You said he's been playing I'm Alone Because I Love You frequently at the Hall.

Yes, yes. They're playing it all the time. Sweet Emma sings it. It's fine. Jim generally starts playing it when they come in. He's obviously having a bit of a I'm Alone Because I Love You fetish or something at present.
Moonlight and Roses it was before that, when he had a few drinks he played Moonlight Roses. It's great really.
This is a kind of nabala.

It's very, very natural the way he plays. Jim Robinson, to my mind, plays just as well if not better now every night than as on records he made 20 years ago. It's great. He's been one of the highlights listening. Percy Humphries, I'm very impressed with Percy as a fellow who just plays the music very, very naturally as it occurs to him. Some nights he blows out, other nights he plays very casually but always very, very nicely.
Well, you were saying he impressed the crowd last night with certain ways of playing. Yes.

We talked about that earlier. Just standing up, putting a very tight mute in the trumpet playing very, very softly. Very straight really, just playing the melody. But just beautifully, nice subtlety. And that brought the house down more than all the loud when the saints sort of stuff. No clowning or anything. Just very, very quiet. In fact, obviously it's a great, it's a great old lesson there. Make the audience listen. Make them do something. And they appreciate it always.
